name: Particle diagram of an element, a compound or a mixture
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: A rectangle (the container) holding 12 to 30 circles that never overlap. Element: all circles the same size and fill (single atoms), or joined pairs for a diatomic element such as H2 or O2. Compound: touching groups of two or three different circles in a fixed pattern (for example one large and two small for H2O). Mixture: two kinds of free particle, or a particle of an element and a particle of a compound, not bonded to each other. Kinds differ by size and by fill (white, hatched, grey) so that the picture survives photocopying (S12).
params: substance (element of atoms | element of molecules | compound | mixture of elements | mixture of compounds | mixture of element and compound), state (gas | liquid | solid), particle count (8 to 40), compound formula (AB | AB2 | A2B | ...)
scienceChecks: All particles of an element are one kind. Each compound particle holds at least two kinds of atom in the ratio of its formula (2 to 1 for H2O). A mixture has at least two kinds of particle and no bond between them. Circles never overlap.
notes: The same particle box serves the states-of-matter row (particleStates): one symbol with two uses.

name: Models of the atom: plum pudding, nuclear and shell
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: Plum pudding: a large circle with a pale fill, small electrons (marked with a minus sign) scattered inside it, and a label saying that the positive charge is spread through the ball. Nuclear model: a very small central dot or circle for the nucleus (marked with a plus sign) and a few electrons on a wide ring or on separate rings far out. Shell model: the nucleus with the concentric shells of bohrAtom. Labels: nucleus, electron, shell. A line says 'not to scale' on the nuclear and shell pictures.
params: model (plum pudding | nuclear | shell), number of electrons (1 to 10), show labels (boolean), electron mark (dot | cross | minus sign)
scienceChecks: The plum pudding picture has no separate nucleus. In the nuclear and shell pictures the nucleus is much smaller than the atom, and every electron is outside it. The electron count in the picture equals the count the parameter asks for.
notes: Read in the AQA summary of 4.1.1.3 and in an AQA paper that asks which diagram shows the plum pudding model. The AQA pages were read through the search tool, not as the PDF.

name: Alpha-particle scattering experiment
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: On the left a source of alpha particles in a lead block with a narrow slit. A straight beam to a thin gold foil drawn as a vertical strip of small circles (the atoms) with a tiny nucleus dot in each. A curved detector screen round the foil. About eight alpha paths drawn as arrows: most go straight through, two or three bend a little, one bounces back. Each path that bends is bent away from the nucleus it passes (like charges repel).
params: number of paths (5 to 12), show nuclei (boolean), show labels (boolean), show the plum pudding prediction in a second panel (boolean)
scienceChecks: A path that passes closer to a nucleus is bent more. Every bent path bends away from the nucleus. No path enters a nucleus. Most paths are straight. At most one path reverses.
notes: A drawn conclusion box ('most of the atom is empty space; the nucleus is small, dense and positive') is plain text.

name: Bohr model of an atom (electronic structure diagram)
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: Concentric circles for the shells (radii about 28, 48, 68 and 88 u), the nucleus at the centre labelled with the symbol or with the numbers of protons and neutrons, and electrons as small dots or crosses spaced evenly round each ring. The shells fill 2, 8, 8, then the fourth shell (potassium and calcium). The structure can also be written as numbers (2,8,1) in a label.
params: element (Z 1 to 20), show nucleus contents (boolean: symbol only | protons and neutrons), electron mark (dot | cross), outer shell only (boolean), number string label (boolean)
scienceChecks: The electrons on the shells sum to Z. The shells fill 2, 8, 8, 2 in order, and an outer shell has electrons only if the shell inside it is full. The shell count equals the period number. The outer-shell count equals the group number (groups 1 to 7); helium has 2.
notes: 4.1.1.7 asks for the first twenty elements as numbers and as a diagram. The AQA wording was read through the search tool.

name: Electron arrangement of an ion (shell diagram in brackets)
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: The shell diagram of bohrAtom for the ion: a metal ion has lost its outer shell, a non-metal ion has the electrons it gained added to its outer shell. The whole picture sits inside large square brackets with the charge written top right outside them (Na+, Mg2+, Cl-, O2-). Optional before-and-after pair joined by an arrow, the atom on the left and the ion on the right. The electrons that moved are drawn with a different mark (crosses for the gained ones).
params: element (Z 3 to 20), ion charge (automatic from the group, or set), show nucleus contents (boolean), show the atom before the ion (boolean), electron mark (dot | cross)
scienceChecks: Electrons = Z minus the charge for a positive ion, Z plus the size of the charge for a negative ion. The ion's shells match the nearest noble gas (2 | 2,8 | 2,8,8). The sign of the charge matches the element: metals positive, non-metals negative. Charge = protons minus electrons.
notes: Same engine as bohrAtom. The brackets and charge are the marks examiners look for.

name: Nuclear (isotope) notation with mass number and atomic number
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: The element symbol in 18 u text with two small stacked numbers at its left: the mass number above, the atomic number below, right-aligned with each other. An optional charge as a superscript at the right. An optional line under it, 'protons 11, neutrons 12, electrons 11'. The label markup has no stacked left-hand index, so this is a small text symbol.
params: element (Z 1 to 36), mass number (A), charge (optional, -3 to +3), show the particle counts (boolean)
scienceChecks: Mass number >= atomic number. Neutrons = A - Z and is not negative. The atomic number matches the element symbol from a table of the first 36 elements. Electrons = Z minus the charge.
notes: AQA 4.1.1.5 asks students to work out the particle numbers from the two numbers; the exact AQA figure was not visible in the text I read.

name: Isotopes drawn as nuclei (protons and neutrons)
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: A tight cluster of circles for the nucleus: protons marked with a plus sign, neutrons plain. Two or three isotopes of one element side by side (for example hydrogen-1, -2 and -3, or chlorine-35 and -37), each under its nuclear notation. Clusters are packed hexagonally so that the number of circles is easy to count.
params: element (Z 1 to 18), mass numbers (one to three values), show notation (boolean), show counts (boolean)
scienceChecks: The proton count equals Z in every cluster and the neutron count equals A - Z. Isotopes of one element have the same Z and different A. Circles do not overlap. The total circles equal A.

name: Periodic table (outline with groups, periods and metal divider)
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: A grid of 18 columns and 7 rows of square cells (the f-block as two separate rows below). Each cell can show the symbol, the atomic number, the name or the relative atomic mass. Group numbers above (1 to 7 and 0, or 1 to 18), period numbers at the left. A stepped line separates metals from non-metals. Highlights: one group, one period, one element (a ring), the transition metals, or a block. Regions use a pattern as well as a fill so that they survive photocopying.
params: cell content (symbol | number | name | blank), range (first 20 | first 36 | all 118), highlight group, highlight period, highlight element, divider line (boolean), region shading (none | metal and non-metal | blocks), group numbering (0 to 7 | 1 to 18)
scienceChecks: The elements run in order of atomic number with the correct group and period. Helium is in group 0. The divider runs between the correct pairs of cells. Transition metals sit in groups 3 to 12 of periods 4 to 7. At most one highlight style is on a cell.
notes: It is a table, but a fixed 118-cell layout with highlight parameters, so it is classed as a symbol, not a chart. James to confirm.

name: Mendeleev's early periodic table with gaps
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: A table of rows and columns of element symbols in order of atomic weight with a few question marks where elements were then unknown (the gaps that predicted gallium and germanium). Used as a source in a question, seldom drawn by a student.
params: show the gaps (boolean), highlight swapped pairs such as tellurium and iodine (boolean)
scienceChecks: none
notes: Table: outside PracDraw unless James brings tables into scope. Content is from memory.

name: Table of relative charge and mass of the subatomic particles
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: A three-row table: proton (relative charge +1, relative mass 1), neutron (0, 1), electron (-1, very small, about 1/1835). Usually a 'complete the table' question.
params: show answers (boolean), which cells are blank
scienceChecks: Charges sum to zero for a neutral atom with equal protons and electrons. The mass of the electron is shown as very small, never as 1.
notes: Table: outside PracDraw unless James brings tables into scope. From memory; a text box with a ruled grid in the editor does the job today.

name: A Group 1 metal reacting with water
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: A trough or a large beaker of water (Water preset, 60 %). A small piece of metal (the irregularSolid symbol made small and pale grey) on the surface, a few bubbles under it, and an optional lit splint above the bubbles. With universal indicator the liquid is the Purple preset to show an alkali. A label gives the metal and the gas (hydrogen).
params: container (trough | beaker), metal (lithium | sodium | potassium), indicator colour (boolean), splint (boolean)
scienceChecks: The metal sits on the liquid surface, not in it. Bubbles are under or beside the piece. If the indicator is on, the liquid is purple or blue, never red or green.
notes: A new template from existing symbols (trough, beaker, irregularSolid, splint). Schools often show a video, so the picture is for a worksheet.

name: Halogen displacement reactions in test tubes
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: Use the testTubeReactions template with three or four tubes in a rack. Tubes hold potassium chloride, bromide or iodide solution (Colourless solution preset) and, after adding a halogen water, the Orange preset (bromine) or the Brown preset (iodine). Label each tube with the pair of chemicals. A tube where nothing happens keeps its first colour.
params: pairs of halogen and halide (Cl2 or Br2 or I2 with Cl- or Br- or I-), result colours
scienceChecks: A displacement happens only when the added halogen is higher in the group than the halide ion (Cl2 with Br- or I-; Br2 with I-). A non-reaction tube keeps its first colour. Bromine water is orange and iodine solution is brown.
notes: No new code. The colour presets already exist.

name: Graph of a property down a group (melting or boiling point)
subject: chemistry
topic: Atomic structure and the periodic table
draw: A line graph or bar chart of melting point or boiling point against the elements of Group 1 or Group 7, used to predict a missing value. Axes, scale and plotted points.
params: group (1 | 7), property, which value is missing
scienceChecks: The trend is monotonic: melting and boiling points fall down Group 1 and rise down Group 7.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. From memory.

name: Particle diagrams of a solid, a liquid and a gas
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Three boxes side by side. Solid: touching circles in a regular lattice, with small vibration marks. Liquid: touching circles in an irregular arrangement filling the lower part of the box, with a few short motion arrows. Gas: widely spaced circles all through the box, with longer arrows in random directions. Each box has a one-line label (arrangement, movement) when asked. Circles do not overlap.
params: state (solid | liquid | gas), particle count (10 to 40), particle kind (atom | pair | triple), show motion arrows (boolean), show labels (boolean)
scienceChecks: A solid is a regular lattice in contact. A liquid has contact without regular rows. A gas has gaps larger than a particle diameter. The three boxes show the same number of particles. Circles never overlap.
notes: The same symbol as particleElementCompoundMixture. Exam questions ask students to state limitations of this model (spacing and size not to scale, no forces shown), which is text.

name: Changes of state (melting, freezing, boiling, condensing, sublimation)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Three particle boxes (solid, liquid, gas) in a row with a pair of labelled arrows between solid and liquid (melting above, freezing below) and between liquid and gas (boiling or evaporating above, condensing below). An optional long curved arrow from solid to gas for sublimation. Arrows are labelled with the change of state and, optionally, 'energy in' on the upward arrows and 'energy out' on the downward ones.
params: show sublimation (boolean), show energy labels (boolean), label mode (names | blank for a worksheet)
scienceChecks: Melting, boiling and sublimation arrows carry 'energy in'; freezing and condensing carry 'energy out'. The boxes use the particleStates arrangements. The arrows join the correct pairs of boxes.

name: Heating and cooling curve of a pure substance
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Axes: temperature (vertical) against time (horizontal). A line that rises, flattens at the melting point, rises again, flattens at the boiling point, rises again; regions labelled solid, solid and liquid, liquid, liquid and gas, gas. The cooling curve is the reverse.
params: direction (heating | cooling), substance (generic | water), show state labels (boolean), show particle boxes under each region (boolean)
scienceChecks: The flat sections lie at the melting point and the boiling point. The temperature never falls during heating. The boiling-point plateau is higher than the melting-point plateau.
notes: Graph: outside PracDraw unless James brings graphs into scope. The priority is how often it is drawn, not a build order. A particle box under each region would use particleStates.

name: Dot-and-cross diagram of an ionic compound
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Two forms. Transfer: the metal atom and the non-metal atom as circles for their outer shells, the metal's electrons as dots and the non-metal's as crosses, with curved arrows showing the electrons moving across. Ions: each ion inside large square brackets with its charge top right outside them; the metal ion shows its full inner shell only (or no outer electrons), the non-metal ion a full outer shell of dots and crosses. For MgCl2 or Na2O the second ion is drawn beside the first with the ratio visible. Inner shells are optional and, when drawn, appear as plain circles.
params: metal (Li | Na | K | Mg | Ca), non-metal (O | S | F | Cl | Br), stage (transfer | ions), show inner shells (boolean), mark style (dot and cross | all dots)
scienceChecks: Electrons lost by the metal atoms equal electrons gained by the non-metal atoms. Each ion has the electron structure of a noble gas. The charge follows the group number (group 1 +1, group 2 +2, group 6 -2, group 7 -1). The numbers of ions give a neutral compound.
notes: AQA 4.2.1.2 limits the examples to Group 1 and 2 metals with Group 6 and 7 non-metals. Brackets and charges are what a mark scheme rewards. Decision for James: whether every picture uses dots for one atom and crosses for the other, and whether another pair of marks is allowed for photocopy-safe prints.

name: Dot-and-cross diagram of a simple covalent molecule
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: One circle for the outer shell of each atom, overlapping where atoms are bonded. Each shared pair sits in the overlap as one dot and one cross. The other outer electrons of each atom stay on its own circle as dots or crosses, with lone pairs drawn as pairs. The central atom is in the middle for H2O, NH3, CH4 and CO2. Double and triple bonds have two and three pairs in the overlap. Inner shells are never drawn. A second layout puts the atoms apart with the shared pairs between them.
params: molecule (H2 | Cl2 | O2 | N2 | HCl | H2O | NH3 | CH4 are the eight in the specification; CO2 | HF | F2 | C2H4 | C2H6 as extras), layout (overlapping circles | circles apart), mark style (dot and cross | all dots)
scienceChecks: Every atom ends with a full outer shell (2 for hydrogen, 8 for the others). The shared pairs equal the usual valency (H 1, Cl 1, O 2, N 3, C 4). The total outer electrons equal the sum over the atoms (8 for H2O, 8 for NH3, 8 for CH4). Lone pairs are shown. Each shared pair has one dot and one cross.
notes: AQA names eight molecules. Examiners expect lone pairs to be shown. A dot-and-cross shows no shape; that limitation is part of the specification.

name: Displayed formula of a small molecule (lines for bonds)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Atom symbols in 15 u text joined by single lines, double lines or triple lines, laid out flat with the bonds at right angles or at 120 degrees (the 2D convention, not the real shape). Hydrogen atoms are shown. Used for H2, HCl, H2O, NH3, CH4, CO2, N2, O2 and the first alkanes.
params: molecule (from a list of 12 small molecules), show lone pairs (boolean), show the molecular formula under it (boolean)
scienceChecks: Each atom has the number of bonds of its valency (H 1, O 2, N 3, C 4, Cl 1). The count of each element equals the molecular formula. Double and triple bonds drawn as two and three parallel lines.
notes: The same bond graph also feeds the ball-and-stick and the organic displayed-formula rows. One molecule engine, several drawings.

name: Ball-and-stick model of a small molecule
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Spheres joined by sticks, drawn as circles with a small highlight line (no shading, no gradient, S7) and sticks as two parallel lines in an oblique view. Methane tetrahedral, ammonia pyramidal, water bent, carbon dioxide and hydrogen chloride linear. Atoms are told apart by size and by a hatch or grey fill, with a key (symbol and fill) beside the model.
params: molecule (from the list of 12 small molecules), view (front | oblique), show key (boolean), show element labels on the balls (boolean)
scienceChecks: The number of balls of each element equals the formula. Each ball has its valency of sticks. Bond angles in the model: 109.5 for CH4, about 107 for NH3, about 104.5 for H2O, 180 for CO2 and HCl. Key matches the fills used.
notes: AQA asks students to name limitations of ball-and-stick models (the sticks suggest physical links, sizes are not to scale). Decision for James: how a 3D model is drawn in a 2D line style (oblique projection).

name: Space-filling model of a small molecule
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Overlapping circles at the atom positions with the nearer atoms drawn in front, and a key for the atoms. No sticks. Mentioned beside dot-and-cross and ball-and-stick when students compare models.
params: molecule (from the list of 12 small molecules), show key (boolean)
scienceChecks: The number of circles of each element equals the formula. Circle sizes follow the relative sizes of the atoms (H smaller than O smaller than Cl).

name: Giant ionic lattice in two dimensions
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: A square grid of touching circles in alternating kinds: the positive ions small and marked +, the negative ions larger and marked -. Usually 4 by 4 to 6 by 6, with a wavy edge or open ends to show that it goes on. A ball-and-stick variant joins neighbours with short lines. Optional ion labels (Na+ and Cl-). For a 1 to 2 compound the layout is staggered, so that a student can count the ratio and give the empirical formula.
params: compound ratio (1 to 1 | 1 to 2 | 2 to 1), ion labels (Na+ and Cl- | Mg2+ and O2- | custom), grid size (3 to 8), style (balls | ball-and-stick | open ends), show charges (boolean)
scienceChecks: No two like ions touch in a 1 to 1 grid. Counting the ions of each kind in the complete repeating unit gives the ratio of the formula. The total charge of the repeating unit is zero. Ion sizes: negative ions drawn larger for the common cases.
notes: AQA names only sodium chloride, but asks students to deduce the formula from a diagram.

name: Sodium chloride lattice in three dimensions (ball and stick)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: A 3 by 3 by 3 cube of alternating small (Na+) and large (Cl-) circles in an oblique projection: the front face drawn square and the back face shifted up and right at half size, joined by lines. Hidden back bonds are thinner or dashed. A variant highlights one central ion and its six neighbours of the opposite kind. The ions are marked + and - and labelled.
params: size (2 by 2 by 2 | 3 by 3 by 3), highlight one ion and its neighbours (boolean), show labels (boolean), hidden lines (dashed | none)
scienceChecks: No two like ions are nearest neighbours along an edge. The highlighted ion has six nearest neighbours of the opposite kind. In a 3 by 3 by 3 block there are 14 ions of one kind and 13 of the other.
notes: Decision for James: the style of 3D structures in a 2D line drawing. Oblique projection with dashed hidden lines is proposed; the same projection serves diamond, ice and iodine.

name: Metallic bonding (positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Rows of equal circles marked + (the metal ions) in a regular lattice, with small dots or minus signs scattered in the gaps between them (the delocalised electrons, drawn irregularly, not in rows). Optional arrows on the electrons for conduction, and optional displaced rows with a slip arrow to show why metals bend.
params: metal (generic | sodium | magnesium | aluminium), rows (3 to 6), columns (4 to 8), show conduction arrows (boolean), show a slip arrow (boolean)
scienceChecks: The delocalised electrons per ion equal the group number (1, 2 or 3), counted over the drawn region. The ion charge equals that number. The ions are one size, regularly spaced. Nothing joins the ions with lines.
notes: Wording of the specification: students recognise metallic structures from diagrams of their bonding.

name: Alloy and pure metal layers (why alloys are harder)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Rows of equal circles for the pure metal, with a heavy arrow showing one layer sliding over the next. The alloy picture is the same lattice with some circles replaced by a larger (or smaller) kind, so the rows are pushed out of line, and the sliding arrow is crossed out. Foreign atoms differ by size and by fill.
params: mode (pure metal | alloy), foreign atom size (larger | smaller), foreign fraction (5 to 30 percent), layers (4 to 7), show slip arrows (boolean)
scienceChecks: The pure picture has one size of circle in straight rows. The alloy picture has at least two sizes and no overlapping circles. The foreign fraction is within the set value.

name: Diamond (giant covalent, tetrahedral)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Carbon atoms (small circles) joined by single lines, each atom bonded to four neighbours in a tetrahedral pattern, in an oblique projection with the rear bonds lighter or dashed. Three sizes: one atom with its four bonds; a cluster of about 14 atoms; a 2D flat network version. Edge atoms end in short stubs, not open bonds. A label gives 'each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds'.
params: extent (one atom | cluster of 14 | cell of 18), view (oblique | flat network), show bond angle (boolean)
scienceChecks: Every interior carbon has four bonds. Bond lengths are equal in the model. The angle between bonds from one atom is 109.5 degrees in the 3D model before projection. No ring has other than six atoms in the cluster.
notes: The specification asks students to explain the properties of diamond, not to draw it; exam figures still show it for recognition.

name: Graphite (layers of hexagons)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Three stacked layers drawn as flat parallelograms in oblique view, each a network of carbon hexagons with atoms at the corners. The top layer is fully drawn, the lower ones are simpler. The gap between layers has dotted lines for the weak forces. Optional dots above one layer for the delocalised electrons. Labels: layer, weak forces, delocalised electron.
params: layers (2 to 4), hexagons per layer shown (4 to 7), show weak forces (boolean), show delocalised electrons (boolean)
scienceChecks: Every atom in a layer has three bonds at 120 degrees and every ring has six atoms. The spacing between layers is clearly larger than a bond. The weak forces are dotted or dashed, never drawn as bonds.

name: Graphene (one layer of hexagons)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: A flat honeycomb of carbon hexagons, about 4 rows by 5 columns, atoms at the vertices and bonds as lines, with short stubs or a wavy cut line at the edge. A label gives 'one atom thick'. An optional side-view inset is a single row of circles.
params: rows (3 to 6), columns (3 to 7), show atoms as dots (boolean), side view inset (boolean)
scienceChecks: Every interior atom has three bonds at 120 degrees. Every ring has six atoms. No ring of another size appears.

name: Buckminsterfullerene C60
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: A ball of 60 carbon atoms joined by lines: 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons, each pentagon surrounded by hexagons. Two views: the visible hemisphere with the rear half in a lighter line, or a flat Schlegel-style network with the outer face as the big outline. Label 'C60'. Hollow.
params: view (ball | flat network), show atoms (boolean), shade the pentagons (boolean)
scienceChecks: 60 vertices, 90 edges, 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons (the vertices minus the edges plus the faces equal 2). Every atom has three bonds. Each pentagon touches only hexagons.
notes: The hardest of the carbon pictures to draw by hand; it should be a generated symbol, not hand-edited.

name: Carbon nanotube
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: A cylinder made by rolling the graphene honeycomb, in oblique view: an open or capped end ellipse, the hexagon network on the visible surface, atoms at the vertices. A label gives 'nanotube'. The length is several times the diameter.
params: length in rings (3 to 8), circumference in hexagons (6 to 10), capped ends (boolean), show atoms (boolean)
scienceChecks: Every atom has three bonds. The hexagon pattern wraps round the tube without a gap or an overlap. Length is at least three times the diameter.

name: Silicon dioxide (giant covalent)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: The diamond network with an oxygen atom drawn in the middle of every bond between two silicon atoms. Silicon atoms larger, oxygen smaller, different fills, with a key. Flat 2D network or a 3D cluster of about 5 silicon atoms. Edge atoms end in stubs.
params: view (flat network | oblique cluster), show key (boolean)
scienceChecks: Every silicon has four oxygen neighbours and every oxygen has two silicon neighbours. No Si-Si or O-O bond. The ratio of silicon to oxygen in a large interior region is 1 to 2.

name: Polymer chains (linear, branched and cross-linked)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Several long zig-zag chains of carbon atoms side by side, with hydrogen stubs. Linear chains (HDPE) lie close and parallel. Branched chains (LDPE) have short side chains that keep neighbours apart. Cross-linked chains (thermosetting) have short bridges between chains. Dotted lines between chains show the weak forces. Optional repeating unit in square brackets.
params: type (linear | branched | cross-linked), chains (3 to 6), branch frequency, show weak forces (boolean)
scienceChecks: Every carbon in a chain has two chain bonds and two other bonds. Branches are attached to chain carbons only. Cross-links join two different chains. Linear chains lie closer together than branched ones.
notes: A past AQA paper, reported through the search tool, shows part of the structures of HDPE and LDPE and asks why HDPE is denser. I could not tell which paper, so the row is secondary.

name: Why ionic compounds conduct only when molten or dissolved
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Three particle boxes of + and - ions: solid (ions fixed in a lattice), molten (ions close together but free), dissolved (ions spread apart in water, with water drawn as plain background). Under each, a small cell and bulb symbol that is off for the solid and lit for the other two, or a label 'ions cannot move' and 'ions free to move'.
params: show circuit symbol (boolean), show labels (boolean), compound label
scienceChecks: The solid box is a regular lattice; the other two are not. Positive and negative ions are present in the same numbers in every box (charge balance). The bulb is lit only when the ions are free.

name: Cubes for surface area to volume ratio (nanoparticles and rates)
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: Cubes of side 1, 2 and 3 units (or one cube cut into 8 smaller cubes) in an oblique view, with grid squares on the visible faces, the side length on an edge, and a line of text under each giving the surface area, the volume and the ratio. The same cubes show why a powder reacts faster than a lump.
params: side lengths (1 to 4 values), cut one cube into n by n by n cubes (boolean), show grid squares (boolean), show values (boolean)
scienceChecks: Surface area = 6 x side squared, volume = side cubed, and the printed ratio equals 6 over the side. Cutting a cube into n cubed smaller cubes keeps the volume and multiplies the surface area by n.
notes: 4.2.4 may be chemistry only (not in Trilogy). Course membership is from my memory of the chemistry-only labels and should be checked. The same drawing serves the surface-area factor in rates.

name: Size scale: atoms, nanoparticles and cells on a powers-of-ten line
subject: chemistry
topic: Bonding, structure and the properties of matter
draw: A horizontal line marked in powers of ten from 0.1 nm to 1 mm with labelled objects: atom, small molecule, nanoparticle range (1 to 100 nm), virus, bacterium, cell, hair width. A scale diagram with no data.
params: range of the scale, which objects are shown or blanked
scienceChecks: Each object sits at its size on the log line. Nanoparticles span 1 to 100 nm. Each tick is ten times the last.
notes: A scale line, not a graph of data; classed chart because it is a labelled axis. Course membership and sizes are from memory.
